section.title: The Temptation in the Wilderness
section.sectionRationale: Immediately after the Father names Jesus His beloved Son and the Spirit descends, that same Spirit leads Him into the wilderness to be tested by the devil. Where Israel failed in the desert and the first Adam fell in the garden, the second Adam stands. Each temptation is answered not with power but with the written word of God, and the tempter withdraws until an opportune time.
section.thesis: The Spirit-anointed Son is tested at every point where Adam and Israel fell, and He conquers not by displaying His power but by trusting and obeying the word of His Father, proving Himself the faithful Son who will save His people.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted; the temptation to turn stone to bread; the temptation to gain the kingdoms by worshiping the devil; and the temptation to test God at the temple, after which the devil departs until an opportune time.

units.label: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness
units.note: full of the Spirit, tempted forty days

verses.text: Then Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness,
where for forty days He was {{peirazo|tempted}} by the {{diabolos|devil}}. He ate nothing during those days, and when they had ended, He was hungry.

units.label: Bread alone
units.note: man shall not live on bread alone

verses.text: The devil said to Him, “If You are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”
But Jesus answered, “It is {{gegraptai|written}}: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’”

units.label: All the kingdoms of the world
units.note: worship the Lord your God and serve Him only

verses.text: Then the devil led Him up to a high place and showed Him in an instant all the kingdoms of the world.
“I will give You authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory,” he said. “For it has been relinquished to me, and I can give it to anyone I wish.
So if You {{proskyneo|worship}} me, it will all be Yours.”
But Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’”

units.label: The pinnacle of the temple
units.note: do not put the Lord your God to the test

verses.text: Then the devil led Him to Jerusalem and set Him on the pinnacle of the temple. “If You are the Son of God,” he said, “throw Yourself down from here.
For it is written: ‘He will command His angels concerning You to guard You carefully,
and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone.’”
But Jesus answered, “It also says, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.

peirazo.gloss: To test, try, or tempt. The same word can mean a testing meant to strengthen or a temptation meant to destroy. The Spirit leads Jesus to be tested, yet the tester is the devil who means His ruin. Jesus is genuinely tempted, yet without sin, Hebrews 4:15.

diabolos.gloss: The devil, literally the slanderer or accuser. He is the personal enemy behind the temptations, claiming authority over the kingdoms of the world and seeking to divert the Son from the Father's path. He withdraws only until an opportune time.

gegraptai.gloss: It stands written, a perfect-tense form meaning what was written remains permanently in force. Three times Jesus answers with this word, each time citing Deuteronomy, wielding Scripture as settled, abiding authority against the tempter.

proskyneo.gloss: To bow down and worship, to render homage. The devil offers the kingdoms in exchange for a single act of proskyneo; Jesus refuses, insisting that worship belongs to the Lord God alone, and so keeps the path that leads through the cross to a kingdom rightly won.

basic.context: Right after His baptism, Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where the devil tests Him over forty days. Hungry and alone, He faces three pointed temptations: to turn stone into bread, to gain all the kingdoms by worshiping the devil, and to force God's hand by leaping from the temple. Each time Jesus answers with Scripture. The devil finally leaves Him, but only for now.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative, but it is deeply patterned. Jesus relives the story of Israel, tested forty days as Israel was tested forty years, and He succeeds where they failed, answering each temptation from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's wilderness lessons. He is also the second Adam, tested and faithful where the first Adam fell. Read it as both real history and rich fulfillment.
basic.originalLanguages: The word peirazo means both test and tempt: the Spirit leads Jesus to be tested, yet the diabolos, the slanderer, means His ruin. Three times Jesus answers with gegraptai, it stands written, citing Deuteronomy as settled authority. The devil offers the kingdoms for one act of proskyneo, worship, and Jesus refuses, giving worship to God alone.
basic.typology: Jesus is the true Israel, tested in the desert and proving faithful where the nation grumbled and fell. He is the second Adam, meeting the tempter's twist of God's word with trust and obedience rather than doubt. The forty days recall both Israel's forty years and Moses' forty days, gathering up the story of God's people in one obedient Son.
basic.christ: Jesus refuses to use His power for Himself, to take a shortcut to the kingdoms, or to test His Father's care. He wins not by might but by trusting and obeying the word. In this He is our substitute and our example: the sinless Son who is tempted in every way as we are, yet never sins, and who therefore can help us when we are tempted.
basic.god: God's word is the weapon that overcomes the tempter, showing that Scripture is enough. God the Father is worthy of exclusive worship and single-hearted trust. Even the testing serves God's purpose, proving the Son and preparing Him for His mission, though the tempter intends only harm.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:13, and 6:16 are the three texts Jesus quotes. Genesis 3 shows the first Adam's fall by doubting God's word. Hebrews 4:15 says He was tempted in every way, yet without sin. James 4:7 tells us to resist the devil so he will flee.
basic.oneStory: Where Adam fell in a garden of plenty and Israel fell in a desert of want, the second Adam and true Israel stands firm. By trusting His Father's word rather than grasping for bread, power, or proof, Jesus begins to reverse the fall and to walk the obedient road that will lead to the cross, the throne, and the salvation of His people.

context.literary:
Luke 4:1-13 is the hinge between the opening of the Gospel and the ministry proper. It is bracketed by two statements about the Spirit: Jesus is 'full of the Holy Spirit' and 'led by the Spirit' in verse 1, and He returns 'in the power of the Spirit' in verse 14. The testing sits inside the Spirit's leading, not outside it. It also sits between two statements of sonship. The Father's voice at the Jordan says, 'You are My beloved Son,' Luke 3:22, and the genealogy that follows closes with 'the son of Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38. The devil's twice repeated 'If You are the Son of God' picks up exactly that thread. The scene is the question of what kind of Son this will be.

The three temptations are built as a matched set. Each has the same shape: a proposal from the devil, a reply from Jesus introduced by Scripture, and a move to a new place. Each reply is taken from Deuteronomy 6 to 8, the stretch of Moses' sermon where Israel is told how to live after the wilderness years. The third round is the only one in which the devil quotes Scripture himself, and it is the one Luke puts last. Matthew's Gospel orders the second and third differently, with the temple before the mountain, Matthew 4:5-10. Luke's sequence moves from the desert to a high place to Jerusalem, and Jerusalem is the city where his Gospel will end. Luke is a writer who arranges by theme and geography, and that choice points the temptation scene toward the city of the cross.

The closing line is a quiet cliffhanger. The devil 'finished every temptation' and 'left Him until an opportune time,' verse 13. The word for time, kairos, marks a season rather than a clock moment, and the reader is told to watch for its return. Luke 22:3 records Satan entering Judas, and Jesus can say in Gethsemane, 'this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness,' Luke 22:53. The wilderness was round one, not the whole contest.
context.historical:
The forty days placed Jesus inside Israel's memory. Moses was on the mountain 'forty days and forty nights without eating bread or drinking water,' Exodus 34:28, and Moses repeats the point in Deuteronomy 9:9. Elijah walked forty days to Horeb on the strength of one meal, 1 Kings 19:8. Behind both stood the forty years in which the whole nation was led through the desert 'to humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart,' Deuteronomy 8:2. A first century Jew who heard that Jesus was in the wilderness for forty days, hungry, would hear Israel's own story being replayed.

The wilderness itself was a place of ambiguity. The Judean desert east of Jerusalem is stark, dry and empty, a landscape where Israel had met God and where Israel had also grumbled. Prophets had promised that God would lead His people back through such a place, and John the Baptist had just drawn crowds out into it. For the people of Luke's day, the wilderness was both the place of testing and the place where the new thing was expected to begin.

The offer of the kingdoms made political sense to the first hearers. Israel lived under Roman rule, and many hoped for a Messiah who would take power by force and break the occupation. The devil's 'authority over all these kingdoms and all their glory' is the shortcut every messianic movement was tempted to take. John's Gospel shows a crowd trying to seize Jesus to make Him king by force, John 6:15, and Peter later tries to steer Him away from suffering, Matthew 16:22-23. These were live pressures, not hypothetical ones.

The pinnacle of the temple placed the third test in public space. The exact spot is uncertain, though the tradition favours the southern edge of the temple complex, where the walls fell steeply into the valley below. Jesus is being invited to stage a rescue in the holiest place in the nation, before the eyes of the faithful. A sign like that would have fitted the expectations of many who looked for a spectacular deliverer.
context.canonical:
The scene looks backward in a chain. Adam, formed from the ground and called God's son by Luke's genealogy, was tested in a garden of plenty and failed, Genesis 3:6. Israel, called God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22, was tested in a desert of want and failed in exactly the three areas Jesus now faces: hunger, when they demanded food and grumbled, Exodus 16:3; worship, when they made the golden calf, Exodus 32:1-4; and testing God, when they asked at Massah, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. Paul reads Israel's wilderness as a set of warnings, naming idolatry, testing Christ and complaining as the pattern to avoid, 1 Corinthians 10:1-13. Jesus meets each of those temptations and passes where they fell.

The temptation story also reaches forward. Hebrews builds a doctrine of Christ's priesthood on it, saying He 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and that because He suffered when tempted 'He is able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18. The cross carries the same words back to Him. The rulers sneer, 'let Him save Himself if He is the Christ of God,' and the soldiers say, 'If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself,' Luke 23:35-37. The devil's 'If You are the Son of God' returns through human mouths, and Jesus again refuses the shortcut.

Other passages show the Messiah receiving the nations by a different road. Psalm 2:7-8 gives the Son the nations as an inheritance when He asks the Father, and Philippians 2:8-11 shows the Father exalting the Son after obedience to death. Colossians 2:15 says that at the cross He 'disarmed the powers and authorities,' and 1 John 3:8 says the Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil.' The wilderness is where that war is first joined in the open.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote so that readers might know the certainty of what they had been taught, Luke 1:4, and this scene does that by showing what kind of Son and Messiah Jesus is before He does a single public deed. Luke wants his readers to see that Jesus' power and identity are never used for His own comfort. The Spirit who descended at the Jordan is the Spirit who leads Him into hunger, and His obedience under pressure is the foundation of every later miracle and sermon.

For Luke's first readers, many of them Gentile believers who had once served other powers, the scene also draws a line around worship. There is one Lord, and a kingdom received by bowing to anyone else is no kingdom. For Jewish readers it shows a Messiah who does not repeat Israel's failure.

Luke also meant this to be a pattern for his readers' own struggles. The devil's methods are carefully described, and so is Jesus' defence. The reader is shown how the weapons work: a clear grasp of what God has actually said, held against a clever misuse of the same words. The scene ends with the devil defeated for now and Jesus ready for ministry, and Luke wants his audience to carry that confidence into the testing they themselves face.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes an event that only Jesus could have lived. It does not command believers to fast for forty days, to go alone into a desert or to expect the devil in visible form. Nor does it teach that every hardship is a direct attack from the devil. The same Spirit who led Jesus into the wilderness also led Him out, and the story is about a particular Son at a decisive hour.

What does carry over is the method. When Jesus answers, He does not argue from His own cleverness or from His status. He quotes what has been written and places it in context. The devil's quotation of Psalm 91 shows that Scripture can be used as a weapon by the wrong person for the wrong aim, and a verse pulled out of its setting can be made to say what God never meant. Believers are told to resist the devil, James 4:7, and to put on the Spirit's sword, which is the word of God, Ephesians 6:17, but the pattern is to know Scripture whole, not to use it as a slogan.

Hebrews also draws a clear application: Jesus' temptation is not a standard we must reach by our own strength but a reason to come to Him for mercy and help in time of need, Hebrews 4:15-16.

debates.question: Could Jesus have sinned?

views.label: He was able not to sin, and could in principle have sinned
views.case: This view takes the language of real testing at face value. Hebrews says He 'was tempted in every way that we are,' Hebrews 4:15, and that He 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. If sin was not even possible, some argue, the struggle would be a pretence. Advocates add that Adam was made without a sinful nature and still fell, so a sinless nature does not by itself guarantee success.

views.label: He was not able to sin
views.case: This has been the main stream of the church's teaching. It rests on the unity of His person: the Son of God cannot be tempted by evil, James 1:13, and the one person who is both God and man cannot act against the Father's will. Defenders say the temptation was real because the pressure was real. A strong wall can be attacked without being breached, and the fact that He did not yield shows how deep the attack went.

views.label: The question goes beyond what the text asks
views.case: Some hold that Scripture says clearly that He was tempted and did not sin, and then stops. The aim is comfort, Hebrews 2:18, not metaphysics, and both of the other views risk saying more than the Bible does.

debates.bearing: All three agree on what Luke cares about: the testing was genuine, the victory was His own obedience to the Father's word, and He is able to help those who are tempted. The more important reading is not whether sin was hypothetically possible but that the second Adam did not fail.

debates.question: Why does Luke reverse Matthew's order of the second and third temptations?

views.label: Luke arranges by his own theme
views.case: Luke ends on the temple in Jerusalem, the city toward which his Gospel moves, Luke 9:51, and where it closes, Luke 24:52-53. Many scholars think he has deliberately placed the climax there. Luke frequently arranges material by theme rather than strict sequence, as Luke 1:3 'orderly account' allows.

views.label: Matthew arranges by his own theme
views.case: Matthew has the mountain last, which fits his pattern of mountain scenes and his ending, where the risen Lord has 'all authority' on a mountain in Galilee, Matthew 28:16-18. On this reading it is Matthew who moved it, and Luke preserved the original order.

views.label: Both are accurate summaries of the same three tests
views.case: Neither writer says 'then' to mark strict sequence in the way a modern diary would. Luke's 'And' is looser than a stopwatch. If the devil's rounds were not strictly numbered, both accounts report the same tests.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the meaning depends on the choice. The three temptations are the same in both Gospels, and the ordering that each writer uses serves his own emphasis.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'led' in verse 1 is in the imperfect tense, and 'being tempted' in verse 2 is a present participle. Luke paints a continuing action: Jesus was being led by the Spirit throughout the forty days, and the testing was ongoing rather than a single moment. Mark's account says the Spirit 'drove' Him out, Mark 1:12, which is stronger. Luke's gentler word keeps the Spirit's leadership in view without softening the fact of the testing.

The devil's two-part approach turns on the phrase 'If You are the Son of God.' He is not doubting the fact, for he has just heard the Father's voice declare it. He is proposing what a Son should do with His sonship. The test is whether Sonship means self-service. Jesus answers by quoting Deuteronomy 8:3, in which the whole point is that Israel's sonship was to be learned through dependence. The Hebrew of that verse says that man lives on what comes from the mouth of the LORD, and Luke's wording of the reply stops at 'bread alone.' The BSB shows that Matthew's version carries the longer clause, 'but on every word that comes from the mouth of God,' Matthew 4:4. Luke's shorter form leaves the reader to supply the rest from the passage Jesus was quoting.

The devil's claim in verse 6 uses a perfect passive verb, 'it has been relinquished' or 'handed over,' which describes a settled state. The verb is paradidomi, the same verb Luke uses of Jesus being handed over to sinners, Luke 9:44 and 24:7. The devil says the world's authority has been handed to him, and he offers to hand it to Jesus. Jesus does not dispute the claim, which fits Scripture's description of a world lying under the evil one's influence, John 12:31, but He denies that the way to the kingdom runs through worship of anyone but the Father.

In Jesus' reply to the second temptation the order of the words matters. Deuteronomy 6:13 in the BSB reads 'Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only,' while Luke 4:8 reads 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.' Jesus' wording places worship, the very thing the devil asked for in verse 7, in the place of fear, and puts the weight on the word 'only.' The devil asked for one act of homage; the reply claims the whole of life as service.

The third reply uses a compound verb. 'Do not put the Lord your God to the test' translates a compound form of the verb for testing, and the sense is to push God until He proves Himself. It is quoted from Deuteronomy 6:16, which adds 'as you tested Him at Massah,' pointing back to Exodus 17:7, the place where the people tested the LORD by asking 'Is the LORD among us or not?'

Last, the devil's quotation from Psalm 91 in verses 10 and 11 has a clipped ending. Psalm 91:11 says the angels will guard 'you in all your ways,' and Luke 4:10 omits the phrase 'in all your ways.' What the devil leaves out is the very boundary of the promise: protection on the Lord's paths, not on a path of showy self-endangering. The word 'pinnacle' is pterygion, a diminutive of the word for wing, and it suggests a small projection or edge high on the temple complex.

typology.type: Israel's forty years in the wilderness
typology.fulfillment: Israel was God's son, called out of Egypt, Exodus 4:22, and led through the desert to learn what was in its heart, Deuteronomy 8:2. It hungered and grumbled, bowed to a calf and tested God at Massah. Jesus is the true Son who enters the same desert and answers each of those failures from the same book. Matthew applies the pattern when he reads Hosea 11:1 of Jesus, Matthew 2:15, and Paul treats Israel's wilderness as a set of warnings, 1 Corinthians 10:1-13. The escalation is that Jesus does not merely avoid their sins but leads His people through the testing. The type has a limit: Israel's failure was corporate and ongoing, while Christ's success is personal and substitutionary, counted to those united to Him.

Luke's genealogy ends with 'the son of Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38, and the very next scene is a test. Adam heard a question about what God had said, Genesis 3:1, and reached for what looked good for food, pleasing to the eye and desirable for wisdom, Genesis 3:6. Jesus answers each appeal differently, and so His obedience undoes the first man's fall. Paul states the exchange directly: 'through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. The pattern is not perfect in every way, since Adam fell in a place of plenty while Jesus stood in a place of need, and that difference makes His victory all the more striking.

typology.type: Moses on the mountain for forty days
typology.fulfillment: Moses spent forty days without bread or water in the presence of God, receiving the covenant, Exodus 34:28 and Deuteronomy 9:9. Jesus spends forty days without food, and the word He lives on is the word that comes from God's mouth. Moses mediated a covenant for a people who soon broke it. The correspondence shows Jesus as the prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15, but greater, since He does not come down to a broken covenant but goes on to establish a new one in His blood, Luke 22:20. It is a pattern of forty days and obedience, though Moses stands as the servant and Jesus as the Son, Hebrews 3:5-6.

typology.type: The kingdom and the shortcut it refuses
typology.fulfillment: The devil offers the kingdoms without suffering. The Father had already promised the Son the nations, Psalm 2:8, but along a road that passes through the cross. Jesus takes that road, and on it receives what the devil offered cheaply: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18. Philippians 2:8-11 shows the order, obedience to death and then the name above every name. The type is partial because the devil's kingdoms were offered as a gift and a trap, while the Father's gift is real and costly.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by showing who He is when no one is watching. Before the crowds, the healings and the sermons, the Son is alone in the desert with nothing but the Father's word. What He refuses tells us what He is. He refuses to make His sonship a means of comfort, to receive the kingdoms without the cross, or to demand proof of His Father's care. In each refusal He takes the path of dependence that Israel and Adam would not.

It leads to Christ as the substitute. Adam's disobedience made many sinners, and Christ's obedience makes many righteous, Romans 5:19. Each temptation was a point at which the human race had failed, and He met it as the representative of a new humanity. Paul can say that God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The righteousness credited to the believer is the righteousness first lived out in places like this one.

It leads to Christ as the sympathizing high priest. Hebrews 4:15 says that we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every way, yet without sin. His holiness did not insulate Him from the pressure; because He did not give way, He felt the full force of it, as a person who holds a rope until the end knows its strain better than the person who lets go. Hebrews 2:18 draws the comfort: because He suffered when tempted, He is able to help those who are tempted.

It leads to Christ as the one who disarms the enemy. The devil is here the 'strong man,' but Jesus will bind him, Luke 11:20-22. The scene sets the pattern for the ministry that follows: demons will cry out His name and be silenced, and the power of the evil one will be pushed back wherever the kingdom comes. At the cross Colossians 2:15 says He 'disarmed the powers and authorities, made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross,' and 1 John 3:8 says He came to destroy the works of the devil. The defeat that began in the wilderness is finished on the tree.

The scene also looks forward to the cross in a more specific way. The kingdoms are offered without suffering, and Jesus will receive them through suffering. The call to leap from the pinnacle is a call to a rescue without a death, and Jesus will wait on the Father's will in Gethsemane: 'Yet not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42. He had told His disciples to 'pray that you will not enter into temptation,' Luke 22:40, and He Himself did.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The stone and the bread are not secret pictures of the Eucharist, and the pinnacle is not a symbol of the church's pride. The links above rest on what Luke and the rest of the New Testament say outright: the Sonship of 3:22 and 3:38, Israel's wilderness, the war with the devil and the high priest who knows our struggle.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that His word is enough. The devil's three proposals each look reasonable and each cut against what God has said. Jesus does not meet them with a new revelation or a display of power. He meets them with passages Israel already had. The same Scripture that was available to the nation in the desert, and which they failed to keep, is shown to be sufficient for the Son. It tells us that God's word is not an ornament for religious people but the living thing that people live on, Deuteronomy 8:3.

The passage also shows God's exclusive claim to worship. The devil's offer is a bargain: one act of homage for all the kingdoms. The reply, from Deuteronomy 6:13, rests on the jealous holiness of the LORD, who in the same passage says, 'the LORD your God, who is among you, is a jealous God,' Deuteronomy 6:15. God cannot be one of several loyalties. That is why the first commandment stands first and why Scripture treats idolatry as the root sin. A God who shared worship would not be God at all.

The passage shows God's goodness and His way with testing. James teaches that God does not tempt anyone, James 1:13, and yet the Spirit leads Jesus into the place where the devil tests Him. Both are true. The devil tempts to destroy; God permits the testing in order to prove and strengthen. Deuteronomy 8:2 says that God tested Israel 'to know what was in your heart,' and the same pattern appears here, with the opposite result. The very circumstance that Satan intends for ruin God turns to the Son's vindication, a pattern that Joseph states in a sentence, 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good,' Genesis 50:20.

It shows God's sovereignty over the evil one. The devil comes only because the Spirit led Jesus there, and he leaves when the testing is done. The claim to hold the kingdoms is allowed to stand for a moment but is nowhere confirmed. The Bible describes a world where evil is real and strong, and yet the devil is on a lead. This is the reason the passage can be read with peace rather than dread.

It reveals the Father's character as the one who gives the kingdom by a better road. The Father had said, 'Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance,' Psalm 2:8. The devil offered the nations in place of the Father and without the cross, and the Son will not take them from any hand but the Father's. The Father who declared 'You are My beloved Son' at the Jordan does not abandon that Son in the desert. He is present in the word the Son quotes.

There is also a hint of the Trinity. The Father speaks at the baptism, the Spirit fills and leads, and the Son answers from the Father's word. Each person is acting in a way that fits their role, and the unity of purpose between them is clear.

For worship, this means that we serve a God whose word we can stand on and whose claim on us is total. We can come to Him with our own hungers, knowing that His Son has stood where we stand and has not been moved. And we can trust that testing which He permits is not the last word.

crossReferences.note: The source of the first reply. Moses tells Israel that the LORD humbled them and let them hunger, then fed them with manna so they would learn that man lives on every word from the LORD's mouth. Jesus is hungry in the same desert and refuses to make bread for Himself, accepting that the Father's word can sustain Him where Israel complained.

The source of the second and third replies, set side by side in the same stretch of Moses' sermon. The call to fear and serve the LORD alone and the warning against testing Him as Israel did at Massah belong together. Jesus draws from one passage twice because the two temptations share a root, which is to treat God as a means.

The story of Massah behind the third reply. Israel was thirsty and quarrelled with Moses, asking whether the LORD was among them. They tested God by demanding proof of His presence. The devil asks Jesus to stage proof of His Father's care. Jesus refuses to make God demonstrate what He has already promised.

The first temptation, which Luke deliberately recalls through his genealogy of Adam. The serpent questioned what God had said and held out food, a pleasing sight and a wish to be like God. The devil's methods have the same shape in Luke 4, but the second Adam answers from God's word, and the outcome is reversed.

The text the devil quotes in the third temptation. In the psalm these verses promise God's protection for the one who trusts Him, and the devil turns them into a tool for forcing God's hand. Read in the whole psalm, with its call to dwell in the shelter of the Most High, Psalm 91:1, the promise belongs to trust, not to a leap made to prove it.

The pastoral answer to the question why this scene is written. The high priest tempted in every way yet without sin invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and find grace in our time of need. His victory in the desert is not only an example but an open door.

Paul reads Israel's wilderness as written for our warning, naming idolatry, testing Christ and complaining. He then promises that God is faithful and will provide a way out of every temptation. The three tests Jesus passes are the three Israel failed, and Paul shows that the church stands in the same line.

The garden scene where the contest resumes at the opportune time. Jesus tells His disciples to pray not to enter into temptation, and He prays 'not My will, but Yours be done.' The refusal to take a shortcut to the kingdom in the desert is renewed at the hour when the cup is placed before Him.

At the cross the devil's 'If You are the Son of God' is repeated by rulers, soldiers and a criminal: save Yourself. The temptation of the wilderness is taken up again in public mockery, and Jesus faces it by staying on the cross, saving others by not saving Himself.

Describes the result of the war begun in the desert. Having disarmed the powers and authorities, Christ made a public spectacle of them and triumphed by the cross. The devil who withdrew 'until an opportune time' is finally exposed at the moment he seemed to win.

Gives the believer's share in the victory: submit to God, resist the devil, and he will flee. The order matters, since submission comes first. Jesus' own pattern, trusting and obeying the Father before confronting the tempter, is the pattern the church is invited to follow.

The promise behind the devil's offer. The Father says to the Son, 'You are My Son,' and invites Him to ask for the nations. The devil offers the same inheritance without the Father's way. Jesus waits to receive the nations as a gift from the one who named Him Son.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible opens with a man and woman in a garden who are asked to live on God's word and fail. It moves through a nation led through a desert to learn the same lesson and fails again. Luke 4 is the moment the story turns. A Son stands in the place where both failed, and does not fall. The question left hanging since Genesis 3, whether anyone from the human family will trust God where Adam did not, is answered by a man in the desert.

It answers what came before at several levels. It answers Eden: the tempter's offers of food, status and a short path to power are laid out and refused. It answers the wilderness: Israel's forty years of complaint and idolatry are matched by forty days of dependence. It answers the long expectation of a Messiah, by showing that the anointed King will not take the kingdoms by seizing them. The Servant who comes to bring good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, has first learned to be poor, hungry and trusting.

It also sets up what follows. The devil departs only for a time, and the Gospel is a series of small returns: demons recognise Jesus and are silenced, opponents ask for signs, His own disciples urge Him to avoid the cross. The temptation to be a king without a cross recurs at Caesarea Philippi, Matthew 16:22-23, and the temptation to save Himself rings from the cross itself. Each time He gives the same answer. The wilderness shapes the Messiah's way before He walks it.

In the larger story it makes sense of the cross. Because Jesus is the one person who never sinned, His death is not the payment for His own failure but the offering of a faithful Son in place of sinners. The obedience begun here is carried through Gethsemane and finished at Calvary, and the result is life for those who are united to Him, 1 Corinthians 15:45. The first Adam became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.

The new creation completes it. The kingdoms the devil claimed to hold become, in the book of Revelation, 'the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15. The deceiver who led the nations astray is thrown down, Revelation 20:10. The tree of life, shut off in Genesis 3:24, is opened again to those who overcome, Revelation 2:7, and the people of God are no longer in the wilderness. They will have been led through it by the Son who went first, and who is able to help those who are being tempted.

sermon.title: The Temptation of Jesus, Part One
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Luke, this message on Luke 4:1 shows how the devil aimed his temptations at both Christ's true humanity and His messianic mission, seeking to lure Him from the Father's will and the way of the cross, and how Christ would not be dissuaded. A faithful, expository treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: Who led Jesus into the wilderness, and why did He go there?

options.text: The Holy Spirit led Him there to be tested by the devil.
options.note: Verses 1 and 2 say Jesus, full of the Spirit, was led by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil.

options.text: He went to fast and pray in solitude for a season.
options.note: He did fast, but Luke's stated point is that the Spirit led Him there specifically to be tested.

options.text: He wandered there by chance after His baptism.
options.note: It was no accident; the Spirit purposefully led Him into the testing.

options.text: The devil dragged Him there against His will.
options.note: It was the Spirit, not the devil, who led Him, and Jesus went willingly.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer each of the devil's temptations?

options.text: By quoting the written word of God, citing Deuteronomy each time.
options.note: Three times Jesus says it is written and answers from Deuteronomy 8 and 6.

options.text: By rebuking the devil with His own divine authority.
options.note: He is the divine Son, but Luke stresses that He answered with Scripture, not a bare display of authority.

options.text: By performing a miracle to prove He was the Son of God.
options.note: Refusing to prove Himself on demand was part of His victory; He worked no sign for the tempter.

options.text: By negotiating a compromise with the devil.
options.note: Jesus made no compromise; He refused every temptation outright.

quiz.q: What did the devil offer in exchange for worship?

options.text: Authority over all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.
options.note: In verses 6 and 7 he offers the kingdoms if Jesus will worship him.

options.text: Relief from His hunger after the long fast.
options.note: That was the pull of the first temptation, not the offer tied to worship in the second.

options.text: The protection of angels if He leapt from the temple.
options.note: That belongs to the third temptation, not the offer of the kingdoms.

options.text: Nothing; the devil demanded worship for its own sake.
options.note: He explicitly dangled the kingdoms and their glory as the price of worship.

quiz.q: How does Jesus' victory in the wilderness relate to Adam and Israel?

options.text: He stands firm as the second Adam and true Israel, succeeding where they fell.
options.note: Tested like Adam and like Israel in the desert, Jesus obeys where they disobeyed.

options.text: He simply gives us a good example of resisting temptation.
options.note: He is our example, but He is more, our victorious substitute who reverses the fall.

options.text: He shows that temptation is not really dangerous.
options.note: The temptations were real and severe; His victory was hard-won, not a sign that testing is trivial.

options.text: He proves that only extraordinary people can resist the devil.
options.note: The opposite: He wins with Scripture available to all, and equips His people to resist too.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the devil left Him 'until an opportune time'?

options.text: The conflict was not finally over; the tempter would return to oppose Jesus again.
options.note: Verse 13 signals that the struggle continues, reaching its height at the cross.

options.text: The devil was defeated in this round but not yet forever.
options.note: True and close, though the phrase specifically points ahead to renewed assaults, not merely a pause.

options.text: The devil gave up on Jesus entirely from then on.
options.note: The words say the opposite; he withdrew only for a time and would come back.

options.text: Jesus was now beyond any further temptation.
options.note: Luke deliberately notes that testing would come again at an opportune time.

questions: The first temptation came when Jesus was hungry and weak. When are you most vulnerable to temptation, and how might you prepare for those moments before they come?
Jesus met every temptation with 'It is written.' How well do you know the Scriptures you would need to answer the lies you most often hear?
The devil offered a shortcut to the kingdoms that bypassed the cross. Where are you tempted by a shortcut that avoids the harder, faithful road God is calling you to walk?
The whole contest turned on who would receive worship. What competes with God for your worship and single-hearted trust?
Jesus was tempted in every way, yet without sin, so He understands and can help you. How does it comfort you to bring your temptations to a Savior who has faced them and won?

translationNotes.note: Man shall not live on bread alone quotes Deuteronomy 8:3. The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts add but on every word of God, filling out the sense of the Deuteronomy text; Luke's shorter reading still points to living by God's word.
Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only quotes Deuteronomy 6:13. Some later manuscripts add Get behind Me, Satan at the start of the verse; the BSB follows the earlier, shorter text.

The devil himself quotes Scripture, Psalm 91:11-12, about angels guarding God's servant. He cites it out of its trusting context to provoke a presumptuous test, showing that Scripture can be misused, and Jesus answers with Scripture rightly applied, Deuteronomy 6:16.

Luke's order of the temptations differs from Matthew's, ending at the temple in Jerusalem rather than on the mountain. The change fits Luke's Gospel-long movement toward Jerusalem, where the decisive testing and victory will come.
